screens.title: What does + mean for money?
screens.prose: In Python, `a + b` on your own class calls `a.__add__(b)`. Here are two amounts in C++, held as whole pence, as in level 1. Adding them does not build.

options.why: That is Python's name. C++ looks for a function spelt `operator+`.

screens.title: Which side is the object on?
screens.prose: An operator can also be a **member** function: then the object is always its left operand. This `Money` defines `*` as a member.

screens.question: Which declaration makes `3 * fee` compile?

options.text: A free function `Money operator*(int k, Money m)`

options.why: A member operator always has the object on the left, so it only ever gives `fee * 3`.

options.text: A free function `Money operator*(Money m, int k)`
options.why: That is `fee * 3` again. The parameters follow the operands, left to right.

options.text: None: C++ cannot put a class on the right of `*`
options.why: A free function can take its operands in either order.

hints.text: For a member, which operand is the object?
In line 12 the left operand is an `int`.
Only a free function can have an `int` as its first parameter.

feedback.correct: A free function puts the `int` first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the parameters to the operands, left to right.

byKey.member: A member operator always has the object on the left, so it only ever gives `fee * 3`.

explain.text: `fee * 3` calls `fee.operator*(3)`, but `3 * fee` needs a function whose first parameter is an `int`. Only a free function can be that. So write symmetric operators as free functions, for both orders when they differ.

screens.title: Printing with <<
screens.question: Why does `operator<<` return `os`?

options.text: So the next `<<` in the chain has a stream to write to
To hand back a copy of the stream
options.why: It returns a reference. Streams cannot be copied, which is also why `os` is taken by reference.

options.text: To report whether the write worked
options.why: The stream records errors itself. The returned `os` feeds the next `<<`.
`operator<<` writes to the stream rather than returning text. Returning `os` keeps the chain going.

hints.text: `a << b << c` is read as `(a << b) << c`.
The left operand of the second `<<` is whatever the first one returned.
The first call must return the stream itself, so the second call writes to the same stream.

feedback.correct: Each `<<` hands the stream to the next.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read `std::cout << x << y` as two calls, one inside the other.

explain.text: `std::cout << a << b` is `operator<<(operator<<(std::cout, a), b)`. Returning `os` by reference keeps one stream flowing through the chain. Taking `std::ostream os` by value would not compile: the stream's copy constructor is deleted.

screens.title: Equal to the last bit
screens.prose: A first `Price` type stores pounds in a `double`. Its `operator==` compares them directly.
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected 0.1 + 0.2 to equal 0.3. In binary it is 0.30000000000000004, so `==` says no.
Taking `Price` by value is fine for a small type. It compiles and runs.

hints.text: Is 0.1 + 0.2 exactly 0.3 as a `double`?
This line compares two doubles bit for bit.
0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, so the comparison is false and prints 0.

feedback.correct: `==` on doubles is exact, and binary fractions are not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out 0.1 + 0.2 in binary floating point.

byKey.one: You expected 0.1 + 0.2 to equal 0.3. In binary it is 0.30000000000000004, so `==` says no.

explain.text: The fill and the limit print as equal but differ in the last bit. Python's `__eq__` on floats has the same problem. Store prices as whole pence or ticks, and `==` becomes exact.

screens.title: Ordering prices
screens.prose: `std::sort` orders a vector using `<`. So a `Price` in whole pence needs `operator<`. Its `==` must agree: two prices are equal when neither is less than the other, here when their pence match, whatever the venue.

state.caption: Ask prices in pounds, before sorting

screens.question: Write `bool operator<(const Price& a, const Price& b)` and `bool operator==(const Price& a, const Price& b)`, comparing pence only.

hints.text: Compare the `pence` members.
The smallest goes first after sorting.
`return a.pence < b.pence;` and `return a.pence == b.pence;`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-5: Test 5 asks whether a price is less than itself, and expects false. Use `<`, not `<=`: `std::sort` needs a strict order.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 compares the same pence at two venues and expects true. Compare pence only, as `<` does.

explain.text: `std::sort` calls your `operator<` for every comparison it makes. It must be strict: `a < a` is false. And `==` must match it, or a sort and a search will disagree about which prices are the same.

screens.title: Price, then time
screens.prose: An exchange fills resting sell orders by **price-time priority**: the lowest ask first, and at the same price, the earliest. `std::tie` builds a tuple of references, and tuples compare field by field. So `std::tie(a.price, a.time) < std::tie(b.price, b.time)` compares prices, then times.
screens.question: Write `bool operator<(const Order& a, const Order& b)`: true when `a` trades before `b` on the ask side.

explain.text: `std::tie` compares price first and falls through to time only on a tie. For bids you would flip the price test, highest first. A matching engine's queue is exactly this order, kept by a sorted container.

ideas: `a + b` on your type calls `operator+(a, b)`: C++'s spelling of Python's `__add__`. Arithmetic operators take values and return a new value; mutation belongs in `+=`.
A member operator always has the object on the left. Write symmetric operators as free functions, so `3 * fee` works as well as `fee * 3`.
`<` must be strict and agree with `==`; compare whole pence, never doubles. `operator<<` takes and returns `std::ostream&` so output chains.

quiz.question: What happens?

options.text: A compile error: no `operator+` takes a `Pnl` and a `Quantity`

options.why: You expected C++ to add the numbers inside. It looks for an `operator+` that takes these two types, and there is none.
There is no conversion from `Quantity` to `Pnl`, so the only `operator+` cannot be used.

feedback.correct: Separate types turn a unit mistake into a compile error.

explain.text: The only `operator+` takes two `Pnl` values, and a `Quantity` is not one. With plain `long long` and `int`, the sum would quietly be 12800. Small wrapper types make units part of the type.

quiz.question: What happens?

options.text: A compile error: the stream's copy constructor is deleted

options.why: Taking `os` by value would copy `std::cout`. Streams cannot be copied: the copy constructor is `= delete`.

options.text: It prints nothing, because it writes to a copy
options.why: It never gets that far. Copying a stream does not compile.

feedback.correct: Streams are passed by reference because they cannot be copied.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does passing `os` by value require?

explain.text: A by-value parameter is built with the copy constructor, and `std::ostream` deletes it. Write `std::ostream& os`, and return it, so the chain works.
